describes: EU VAT determination: what is charged, and why.

dataset.name: eu-tax-dataset
dataset.why: Vectors pin a committed slice of the published dataset rather than the live mirror. A rate that changes in the world must not silently change what these vectors assert — that would make them a mirror of today's data instead of a description of the engine's behaviour.

vectors.pins: A domestic B2C supply of a class the union reduces nowhere is taxed at the member state's standard rate.
An inclusive price is decomposed, not grossed up. The customer pays what the shelf said.
A reduced band is reached through the published class map, not by the caller naming a rate. France reduces foodstuffs to 5.5% and the caller only ever says 'groceries'.

A class the member state does NOT reduce is charged at standard, and that is an answer rather than a fallback. Hungary taxes groceries at its full 27% — assuming every state reduces food is how a foreign intuition becomes an under-charge.
A cross-border B2B supply to a validated VAT number is reverse charged: no tax, and the invoice must say so.

THE FAIL-SAFE DIRECTION. A business customer whose VAT number was NOT conclusively validated is charged, not zero-rated. An unverified number is not evidence of anything, and under-collection here is unrecoverable.
A negative amount is a credit note and must refund the tax that was charged. It is the same determination with the sign carried through — not an untaxed line.
The rate is the one that applied on the SUPPLY date, not today's. A backdated invoice is priced under the law that was in force when the supply happened.
The Canary Islands sit inside Spain and outside the VAT area. A postcode is the only thing that distinguishes them, because the addressing reference data carries no subdivision for them.

expect.why: Outside the VAT area entirely — IGIC applies locally and is not ours to charge.

vectors.pins: DENY-BY-DEFAULT, AND THE DIRECTION MATTERS. A Danish seller supplying a French consumer is taxed at DESTINATION unless a below-threshold OSS status is affirmatively asserted. Absent any status the general rule applies — silence is not relief. Reading an empty registration list as 'charge nothing' is US thinking: there, no nexus means you must not collect; here, a distance seller is obliged to collect through OSS and not being registered is non-compliance, not an exemption.
Currency minor units are not universally two. A JPY line must not carry cents.

orders.pins: A mid-period plan change is two lines on one document: a credit for the unused part of the old plan and a charge for the new one. Both are the same supply date, so both must resolve the SAME rate — a credit priced at one rate and its replacement at another leaves a residue that reconciles to nothing. This is the billing shape, and it is in the corpus so billing does not end up being the only consumer v1 was designed around.

notModelled.why: THE ENGINE CANNOT EXPRESS THIS YET, and it is the most common line in e-commerce. Article 78(b) makes transport charged by the supplier part of the taxable amount of the supply it accompanies — so delivery on a cart of books is taxed at the books' reduced rate, not the standard one. There is no shipping concept here: a caller must pick a TaxClass for the delivery line, and picking GeneralGoods on a French book order charges 20% where 5.5% is due.
notModelled.openDecision: The directive fixes the principle and is silent on MIXED carts — and so, deliberately, are the member states. HMRC's Notice 700/24 permits 'any fair and reasonable apportionment, which doesn't have to be based on price': value, cost, weight or special delivery requirements all qualify. Denmark's VAT act carries no explicit rule at all; the market-price method is the main one, cost-based where separate prices are absent, and a recent styresignal widened the choice further.
notModelled.notTheSameThing: Colorado's Retail Delivery Fee is modelled and is a different animal: a fixed levy per delivery, not a rate on a charge.
notModelled.thereforeNotOurChoice: So the apportionment basis is NOT ours to hardcode. Baking in pro-rata-by-value would impose a choice that belongs to the taxpayer, and it is wrong in real cases: a heavy zero-rated item shipped alongside a light standard-rated one makes weight defensible where value over-allocates. The design is a caller-supplied policy, pro-rata by net value as the documented default, and the basis actually used recorded in the reason — because 'fair and reasonable' requires it to be STATED and consistent, not merely correct.
